anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.front: Where does the intercostal neurovascular bundle run, and in what order?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.back: In the costal groove at the inferior border of the rib above, ordered top → bottom Vein, Artery, Nerve (“VAN”).

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.front: When inserting a chest drain or aspiration needle, where relative to the rib should you go, and why?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.back: Just above the upper border of the lower rib — to avoid the main neurovascular bundle in the costal groove of the rib above.

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.front: Describe the borders of the “triangle of safety” for chest-drain insertion.
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.back: Anterior border of latissimus dorsi, lateral border of pectoralis major, a line above the 5th intercostal space (nipple level), with the apex at the axilla.

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.front: What are the sources of the posterior and anterior intercostal arteries?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.back: Posterior intercostal arteries → from the thoracic aorta; anterior intercostal arteries → from the internal thoracic artery.

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.front: How does a tension pneumothorax present, and how is it managed?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.back: Respiratory distress, absent breath sounds, hyper-resonance, trachea deviated away, distended neck veins, hypotension. It is a clinical diagnosis → immediate needle/finger decompression (5th ICS, mid-axillary) then a chest drain.

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.front: Which ribs are most commonly fractured, and what does a 1st/2nd rib fracture imply?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.back: The middle ribs (5–9); a 1st/2nd rib fracture implies high-energy trauma (look for great-vessel / brachial-plexus injury).

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.front: A fracture of the lower ribs (9–12) should raise concern for injury to which organs?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.back: The spleen (left) or liver (right), and the kidneys.

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.front: What is a flail chest?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.back: ≥2 adjacent ribs each fractured in ≥2 places → the segment moves paradoxically (inward on inspiration); the underlying lung contusion causes the hypoxia.

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.front: Why is the visceral pleura insensitive to pain but the parietal pleura painful?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.back: Visceral pleura has autonomic innervation (no pain); parietal pleura is supplied by the intercostal (T1–T11) and phrenic (C3–C5) nerves → it is pain-sensitive.

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.front: What is the costodiaphragmatic (costophrenic) recess, and its clinical importance?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.back: The lowest pleural space, not filled by lung in quiet breathing — where pleural effusions collect (blunting the costophrenic angle on X-ray).

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.front: Name the fluid types that can collect in the pleural space.
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.back: Pneumothorax (air), pleural effusion (serous), haemothorax (blood), empyema (pus), chylothorax (thoracic-duct lymph).

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.front: Where do the lung inferior borders and pleural reflections cross the ribs?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.back: Lung borders at ribs 6 (midclavicular), 8 (midaxillary), 10 (paravertebral); the pleura runs two ribs lower — 8, 10, 12.

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.front: How high does the lung apex extend, and why does it matter?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.back: ~2–3 cm above the medial third of the clavicle — so it can be injured during neck procedures (e.g. central line insertion → pneumothorax).

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.front: Why do inhaled foreign bodies usually lodge in the right main bronchus?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.back: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left.

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.front: How many lobes does each lung have?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.back: Right = 3 (upper, middle, lower); left = 2 (upper with lingula, lower) — the left gives room for the heart (cardiac notch).

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.front: Name the diaphragmatic openings and their vertebral levels.
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.back: T8 caval opening; T10 oesophageal hiatus; T12 aortic hiatus (“I 8 ten EGgs AT 12”).

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.front: What passes through the T8, T10 and T12 diaphragmatic openings?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.back: T8 = IVC + right phrenic nerve; T10 = oesophagus + vagal trunks; T12 = aorta + thoracic duct + azygos vein.

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.front: What is the nerve supply of the diaphragm, and the mnemonic?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.back: The phrenic nerve (C3–C5) — motor & sensory. “C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive.”

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.front: Why does irritation of the central diaphragm cause shoulder-tip pain?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.back: The central diaphragm is supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3–C5), so pain is referred to the C4 dermatome — the shoulder tip (e.g. subphrenic abscess, blood, gallbladder disease).

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.front: Give the four cardiac valve auscultation areas.
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.back: Aortic — 2nd ICS right sternal edge; Pulmonary — 2nd ICS left sternal edge; Tricuspid — 4th/5th ICS left sternal edge; Mitral — 5th ICS midclavicular line (apex).

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.front: Match the coronary arteries to their myocardial territories.
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.back: LAD → anterior wall & septum (V1–V4); circumflex → lateral (I, aVL, V5–6); RCA → inferior (II, III, aVF).

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.front: Which coronary artery usually supplies the SA and AV nodes, and its clinical relevance?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.back: The right coronary artery (SA node ~60%, AV node ~90%) → an inferior MI can cause bradyarrhythmia / heart block.

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.front: What is Beck’s triad, and what does it indicate?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.back: Hypotension, raised JVP & muffled heart sounds — indicating cardiac tamponade (± pulsus paradoxus).

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.front: How is cardiac tamponade relieved, and why can it cause shoulder pain?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.back: Pericardiocentesis (subxiphoid, aiming at the left shoulder); the pericardium’s sensory supply is the phrenic nerve → referred shoulder/neck pain.

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.front: What does the sternal angle (of Louis, T4/5) mark?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.back: The 2nd costal cartilage, the tracheal bifurcation, the start & end of the aortic arch, and the boundary between the superior & inferior mediastinum.

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.front: How does superior vena cava obstruction present, and its commonest cause?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.back: Facial & arm swelling, distended neck veins, Pemberton’s sign; usually caused by a lung cancer.

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.front: Name the branches of the aortic arch.
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.back: The brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid and left subclavian arteries.

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.front: Why can an aortic arch aneurysm or apical lung tumour cause hoarseness?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.back: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the arch at the ligamentum arteriosum; compression paralyses the vocal cord (Ortner’s syndrome).

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.front: Name the three oesophageal constrictions and their approximate distances from the incisors.
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.back: Cricopharyngeus (~15 cm), the aortic arch + left main bronchus (~25 cm), and the diaphragmatic hiatus (~40 cm).

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.front: What are the classic features of aortic coarctation?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.back: Radio-femoral delay, upper-limb hypertension, and rib notching (from collateral intercostal vessels) on X-ray.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.front: What three bony elements make up the thoracic cage?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.back: The sternum (anterior), 12 pairs of ribs + costal cartilages (lateral), and the 12 thoracic vertebrae (posterior).

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.front: What bounds the thoracic inlet (superior aperture)?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.back: The body of T1, the 1st pair of ribs and the manubrium.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.front: What closes the thoracic outlet (inferior aperture)?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.back: The diaphragm.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.front: Name the three parts of the sternum.
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.back: The manubrium, the body and the xiphoid process.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.front: What does the sternal angle (of Louis) mark?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.back: The manubriosternal joint = the 2nd costal cartilage (the point to count ribs from), at the T4/5 level (tracheal bifurcation, aortic arch, superior/inferior mediastinal boundary).

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.front: Classify the ribs by their anterior attachment.
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.back: True (1–7) — direct to the sternum via their own cartilage; false (8–10) — to the cartilage of the rib above; floating (11–12) — no anterior attachment.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.front: Describe the features of a typical rib (3–9).
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.back: A head (two facets → its own vertebra + the one above), a neck, a tubercle (facet for the transverse process), an angle, and a shaft with the costal groove on its inferior border.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.front: What is special about the 1st rib?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.back: It is the broadest, shortest & most curved, has a single head facet, and its scalene tubercle separates the grooves for the subclavian vein (anterior) and the subclavian artery + T1 (posterior).

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.front: Which ribs lack a neck and tubercle?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.back: The 11th and 12th (floating) ribs.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.front: With what does the head of a typical rib articulate?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.back: The demifacets of two adjacent vertebral bodies (its own vertebra and the one above) — the costovertebral joint of the head.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.front: With what does the rib tubercle articulate?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.back: The transverse process of its own vertebra — the costotransverse joint.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.front: What type of joint is the 1st sternocostal joint versus the 2nd–7th?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.back: The 1st is a primary cartilaginous (synchondrosis) — immobile; the 2nd–7th are synovial plane joints.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.front: What type of joint is the manubriosternal joint (and what happens to the xiphisternal joint with age)?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.back: The manubriosternal joint is a secondary cartilaginous (symphysis); the xiphisternal joint is cartilaginous and usually ossifies with age.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.front: Describe the three intercostal muscle layers and their fibre directions.
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.back: External — fibres infero-anterior (“hands in pockets”), elevate the ribs (inspiration); internal — infero-posterior, depress the ribs (forced expiration); innermost — deepest layer.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.front: Where does the intercostal neurovascular bundle lie, and in what order?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.back: In the plane between the internal & innermost intercostals, in the costal groove; ordered top→bottom Vein, Artery, Nerve (VAN).

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.front: What are the intercostal nerves, and what is the T12 nerve called?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.back: The intercostal nerves are the anterior rami of T1–T11; the T12 anterior ramus is the subcostal nerve.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.front: Where does the internal thoracic (mammary) artery arise, and how does it end?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.back: From the subclavian artery; it descends behind the costal cartilages and ends by dividing into the superior epigastric and musculophrenic arteries.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.front: What does the internal thoracic artery supply along its course?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.back: The anterior intercostal arteries (upper spaces), plus pericardiacophrenic & perforating branches.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.front: Where do the posterior intercostal arteries arise?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.back: From the thoracic aorta (the upper two spaces from the costocervical trunk).

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.front: Why is the internal thoracic artery clinically important?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.back: The left internal thoracic artery (LIMA) is the gold-standard coronary artery bypass graft (to the LAD).

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.front: Which movement of breathing increases the antero-posterior diameter, and which the transverse?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.back: Pump-handle (upper ribs + sternum up & forward) → antero-posterior; bucket-handle (lower ribs up & out) → transverse.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.front: Which muscle is the main driver of quiet inspiration, and what does it change?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.back: The diaphragm — its descent increases the vertical diameter of the thorax.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.front: Which muscles are recruited in forced inspiration versus forced expiration?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.back: Forced inspiration: scalenes, SCM, pectoral muscles, serratus anterior (accessories). Forced expiration: the abdominal wall muscles + internal intercostals (quiet expiration is passive).

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.front: Is quiet expiration active or passive?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.back: Passive — driven by the elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.front: What forms the costal margin, and where is the subcostal angle?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.back: The 7th–10th costal cartilages; the subcostal angle is at the xiphisternum.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.front: What is a cervical rib and what can it cause?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.back: An extra rib arising from C7 → thoracic outlet syndrome (compression of the lower brachial plexus / subclavian artery).

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.front: What are pectus excavatum and pectus carinatum?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.back: Sternal deformities: excavatum = a sunken sternum; carinatum = a protruding (“pigeon”) chest.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.front: Which intercostal space is the male nipple usually at, and where is the jugular notch?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.back: The nipple ≈ the 4th intercostal space; the jugular (suprasternal) notch ≈ T2.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.front: Where does the trachea begin and where does it bifurcate?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.back: It begins at C6 (cricoid cartilage) and bifurcates at the carina (T4/5, the sternal angle).

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.front: What keeps the trachea patent, and what bridges the posterior gap?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.back: C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings; the posterior gap (against the oesophagus) is bridged by the trachealis muscle.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.front: Give the order of the airways from main bronchus to bronchopulmonary segment.
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.back: Main (primary) → lobar (secondary) → segmental (tertiary) bronchi → bronchopulmonary segments.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.front: Why do inhaled foreign bodies usually enter the right main bronchus?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.back: It is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.front: Describe the lobes and fissures of each lung.
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.back: Right: 3 lobes (upper, middle, lower) with an oblique + horizontal fissure; left: 2 lobes (upper with lingula, lower) with one oblique fissure and a cardiac notch.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.front: What structures pass through the root (hilum) of the lung?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.back: The main bronchus, pulmonary artery, two pulmonary veins, bronchial vessels, nerves and lymphatics.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.front: What does the mnemonic 'RALS' describe at the lung hilum?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.back: The position of the pulmonary artery relative to the bronchus: on the Right it is Anterior, on the Left it is Superior.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.front: What defines a bronchopulmonary segment, and why is it surgically important?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.back: A functionally independent unit with its own segmental (tertiary) bronchus and artery → it can be resected individually (~10 right, 8–10 left).

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.front: Describe the dual blood supply of the lungs.
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.back: The pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood for gas exchange; the bronchial arteries (from the thoracic aorta) supply the lung tissue itself.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.front: What does the right atrium receive, and name two of its internal features.
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.back: It receives the SVC, IVC & coronary sinus; features include the crista terminalis, pectinate muscles and the fossa ovalis.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.front: What is the fossa ovalis a remnant of?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.back: The foramen ovale (the fetal interatrial shunt), which closes after birth.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.front: What is the moderator band and what does it carry?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.back: A muscular band across the right ventricle that carries the right bundle branch to the anterior papillary muscle (speeding its contraction).

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.front: Which chamber has the thickest wall, and where does it pump?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.back: The left ventricle (thickest wall, forms the apex) — it pumps into the aorta.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.front: How many vessels drain into the left atrium, and which?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.back: The four pulmonary veins (two from each lung).

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.front: How are the atrioventricular valves prevented from prolapsing during systole?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.back: By the chordae tendineae anchoring the cusps to the papillary muscles of the ventricular wall.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.front: How do the semilunar valves differ from the AV valves?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.back: The semilunar (aortic & pulmonary) valves have 3 cusps and no chordae; the aortic sinuses give off the coronary arteries.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.front: Name the components of the cardiac conducting system in order.
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.back: SA node → AV node → bundle of His → right & left bundle branches → Purkinje fibres.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.front: Where is the SA node, and what is its role?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.back: In the right atrial wall at the top of the crista terminalis (junction with the SVC); it is the pacemaker.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.front: Why is the AV node/bundle of His so important electrically?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.back: It is the only electrical connection between the atria and ventricles — the fibrous skeleton insulates the rest.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.front: From where do the coronary arteries arise?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.back: From the aortic sinuses (right & left) at the root of the aorta, just above the aortic valve.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.front: What does the right coronary artery supply, including the conducting tissue?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.back: The right heart, the inferior wall (via the posterior descending in right-dominance), and the SA node (~60%) & AV node (~90%).

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.front: What do the LAD and circumflex arteries supply?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.back: LAD (anterior interventricular) → anterior wall & anterior septum; circumflex → lateral wall.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.front: What determines coronary 'dominance'?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.back: Which artery gives off the posterior descending (interventricular) artery — ~70% are right-dominant.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.front: Where does most of the venous blood of the heart drain?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.back: Into the coronary sinus (in the posterior atrioventricular groove) → the right atrium.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.front: Name the layers of the pericardium.
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.back: Fibrous pericardium (tough outer sac) and the serous pericardium — a parietal layer and a visceral layer (the epicardium), with the pericardial cavity between.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.front: Name the two pericardial sinuses and their significance.
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.back: The transverse sinus (between the arterial & venous outflows — used to cross-clamp great vessels) and the oblique sinus (a cul-de-sac behind the left atrium).

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.front: What nerve gives the pericardium its sensory supply, and what results?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.back: The phrenic nerve → pericardial pain is referred to the shoulder.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.front: Where does the oesophagus run, and what muscle types make up its thirds?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.back: From C6 to the cardia at T10/11; the upper third is skeletal muscle, the middle mixed, the lower smooth muscle.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.front: Why do oesophageal varices form in portal hypertension?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.back: The lower-third veins drain to the left gastric → portal system; in portal hypertension this porto-systemic anastomosis dilates into varices.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.front: Where is the thymus, what is its function, and its key association?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.back: In the superior/anterior mediastinum behind the manubrium; it is the site of T-lymphocyte maturation; it involutes after puberty and is associated with myasthenia gravis (hyperplasia/thymoma).

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.front: What are the intercostal nerves, and what is the T12 nerve called?
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.back: The anterior rami of T1–T11; the T12 anterior ramus is the subcostal nerve.

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.front: Which intercostal nerves continue onto the abdominal wall?
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.back: T7–T11 (the thoraco-abdominal nerves), plus the subcostal (T12).

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.front: Name the cutaneous branches of a typical intercostal nerve.
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.back: A lateral cutaneous branch (splitting into anterior & posterior) and an anterior cutaneous branch (plus a collateral branch).

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.front: What does the intercostal nerve supply?
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.back: Motor to the intercostal (and lower abdominal wall) muscles, and sensory to the overlying skin and the parietal pleura/peritoneum.

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.front: Give the key trunk dermatome landmarks (T2, T4, T6, T10, T12/L1).
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.back: T2 = axilla · T4 = nipple · T6 = xiphisternum · T10 = umbilicus · T12/L1 = groin.

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.front: From which roots does the phrenic nerve arise?
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.back: C3, C4 & C5 — “C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive.”

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.front: Describe the course of the phrenic nerve in the thorax.
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.back: It descends on scalenus anterior in the neck, then runs anterior to the lung root between the mediastinal pleura & pericardium (with the pericardiacophrenic vessels) to the diaphragm.

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.front: What are the motor and sensory supplies of the phrenic nerve?
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.back: The sole motor nerve to the diaphragm; sensory to the central diaphragm, the fibrous/parietal pericardium and the mediastinal pleura.

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.front: Why does phrenic-nerve (or central diaphragm/pericardial) irritation cause shoulder-tip pain?
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.back: Its C3–C5 fibres refer pain to the C4 dermatome — the shoulder tip.

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.front: Where does the right phrenic nerve pierce the diaphragm?
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.back: At the caval opening (T8) (it is shorter & straighter than the left).

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.front: What is the relationship of the phrenic and vagus nerves to the lung root?
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.back: The phrenic passes anterior to the root (“phrenic = front”); the vagus passes posterior to it.

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.front: What type of fibres does the vagus carry, and what plexuses does it form in the thorax?
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.back: Parasympathetic (and visceral afferent) fibres; it contributes to the cardiac & pulmonary plexuses and forms the oesophageal plexus.

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.front: What do the vagal trunks become, and where do they pass through the diaphragm?
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.back: The anterior (mainly left) and posterior (mainly right) vagal trunks, passing through the oesophageal hiatus (T10).

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.front: Where does the right recurrent laryngeal nerve loop?
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.back: Under the right subclavian artery.

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.front: Where does the left recurrent laryngeal nerve loop, and why is this clinically important?
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.back: Under the aortic arch (at the ligamentum arteriosum); its long thoracic course means it can be compressed → hoarseness (mediastinal nodes, apical lung tumour, or a cardiovascular cause such as aortic aneurysm / left atrial enlargement — the last being Ortner’s / cardiovocal syndrome).

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.front: What is the sympathetic trunk, and where do its preganglionic fibres arise?
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.back: A chain of paravertebral ganglia running over the rib heads; preganglionic neurons arise from the lateral horn of T1–L2.

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.front: What are white and grey rami communicantes?
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.back: White rami carry preganglionic (myelinated) fibres into the sympathetic chain (T1–L2 only); grey rami carry postganglionic fibres back to every spinal nerve.

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.front: Name the three thoracic splanchnic nerves, their roots and their target ganglia.
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.back: Greater (T5–T9) → coeliac ganglion; lesser (T10–T11) → aorticorenal / superior mesenteric ganglion; least (T12) → renal plexus.

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.front: What is special about the splanchnic nerves’ path through the sympathetic chain?
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.back: They are preganglionic fibres that pass through the chain without synapsing, synapsing instead in the abdominal (pre-aortic) ganglia.

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.front: What are the autonomic effects on the heart (cardiac plexus)?
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.back: Sympathetic → ↑ rate & force, dilates coronaries; parasympathetic (vagus) → ↓ rate.

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.front: What are the autonomic effects on the lungs (pulmonary plexus)?
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.back: Sympathetic → bronchodilation (& vasoconstriction); parasympathetic (vagus) → bronchoconstriction & secretomotor.

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.front: Why is myocardial pain referred to the chest, left arm and jaw?
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.back: Cardiac visceral afferents run back with the sympathetics to the T1–T4/5 spinal segments, so pain is referred to those dermatomes.

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.front: What is Horner’s syndrome and its features?
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.back: Interruption of the sympathetic supply to the head (T1 / stellate ganglion) → ptosis, miosis & anhidrosis (± enophthalmos).

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.front: Horner’s syndrome together with a wasted hand should make you think of what?
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.back: A Pancoast (apical lung) tumour invading the sympathetic chain & the lower brachial plexus.

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.front: Which nerve gives a large branch to the brachial plexus?
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.back: The first (T1) intercostal nerve gives a large branch to the brachial plexus (leaving only a small intercostal nerve).

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.front: What are the parts of the thoracic aorta?
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.back: The ascending aorta, the arch of the aorta, and the descending (thoracic) aorta.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.front: Which arteries arise from the ascending aorta?
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.back: The right & left coronary arteries, from the aortic sinuses just above the aortic valve.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.front: Name the three branches of the aortic arch (in order, right→left along the arch).
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.back: The brachiocephalic trunk, the left common carotid artery, and the left subclavian artery.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.front: What does the brachiocephalic trunk divide into?
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.back: The right common carotid and the right subclavian arteries.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.front: What is the ligamentum arteriosum, and what important nerve relates to it?
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.back: The fibrous remnant of the ductus arteriosus, tethering the aortic arch to the left pulmonary artery; the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under it.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.front: What is the aortic isthmus, and why is it clinically important?
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.back: The slightly narrowed segment between the left subclavian artery and the ligamentum arteriosum — the classic site of coarctation and of traumatic aortic rupture (a tethered point in deceleration injury).

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.front: List the visceral branches of the descending thoracic aorta.
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.back: Bronchial, oesophageal, pericardial & mediastinal branches.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.front: List the parietal branches of the descending thoracic aorta.
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.back: The posterior intercostal arteries (3rd–11th), the subcostal and the superior phrenic arteries.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.front: At what vertebral level does the aorta pass through the diaphragm, and through which opening?
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.back: At T12, through the aortic hiatus (behind the median arcuate ligament).

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.front: What is unusual about the blood carried by the pulmonary arteries and veins?
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.back: The pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood (the only arteries to do so); the pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood (the only veins to do so).

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.front: Describe the pulmonary trunk and its division.
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.back: It leaves the right ventricle and divides into the right & left pulmonary arteries, which carry deoxygenated blood to the lungs.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.front: How many pulmonary veins are there, and where do they drain?
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.back: Four (two per lung); they return oxygenated blood to the left atrium.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.front: How is the superior vena cava formed?
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.back: By the union of the right & left brachiocephalic veins, behind the 1st right costal cartilage; it has no valves and ends in the right atrium.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.front: How is each brachiocephalic vein formed?
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.back: By the union of the internal jugular and subclavian veins (at the venous angle); the left brachiocephalic vein is longer and crosses the midline.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.front: Which vein does the SVC receive just before entering the right atrium?
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.back: The azygos vein (which arches forward over the right lung root).

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.front: At what level, and with which nerve, does the IVC pierce the diaphragm?
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.back: At the caval opening (T8), accompanied by the right phrenic nerve; it then enters the right atrium immediately.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.front: Describe the course of the azygos vein.
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.back: It ascends on the right of the vertebral bodies and arches over the root of the right lung (T4) to drain into the SVC.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.front: What do the hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins do?
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.back: They drain the left posterior thoracic wall (lower and upper respectively) and cross the midline to join the azygos vein.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.front: Why is the azygos system clinically important?
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.back: It is a major cavo-caval anastomosis linking the SVC & IVC systems — in SVC or IVC obstruction it enlarges to provide collateral venous return.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.front: What is the thoracic duct, and where does it begin?
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.back: The largest lymphatic vessel; it begins at the cisterna chyli (~L1–L2) in the abdomen.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.front: Through which diaphragmatic opening does the thoracic duct enter the thorax?
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.back: The aortic hiatus (T12).

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.front: Describe the course of the thoracic duct in the thorax.
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.back: It ascends anterior to the vertebral bodies (between the aorta & azygos), crosses to the left at ~T4/5, and drains into the left venous angle.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.front: Where does the thoracic duct terminate?
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.back: At the left venous angle — the junction of the left internal jugular & left subclavian veins.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.front: Which regions of the body does the thoracic duct drain?
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.back: Everything except the right upper quadrant — i.e. all of the body below the diaphragm plus the left head/neck, left arm and left thorax.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.front: What does the right lymphatic duct drain?
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.back: The right upper quadrant — the right side of the head & neck, the right arm and the right thorax — into the right venous angle.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.front: Trace the lymphatic drainage of the lung.
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.back: Bronchopulmonary (hilar) → tracheobronchial (carinal) → paratracheal → bronchomediastinal trunks.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.front: What is SVC obstruction, its usual cause, and its features?
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.back: Compression/occlusion of the SVC, usually by a lung cancer (or mediastinal mass) → facial & upper-limb swelling, distended non-pulsatile neck veins, and a positive Pemberton’s sign; azygos collaterals develop.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.front: What is a chylothorax, and what causes it?
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.back: Leakage of milky chyle into the pleural cavity from thoracic-duct injury (surgery or trauma).

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.front: Classify aortic dissection and give the management principle.
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.back: Stanford type A involves the ascending aorta (usually surgical); Stanford type B is confined to the descending aorta distal to the left subclavian (usually medical).

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.front: What signs suggest aortic coarctation at the isthmus?
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.back: Radio-femoral delay, upper-limb hypertension with lower-limb hypotension, and rib notching (from dilated collateral intercostal arteries).

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.question: In what order do the vein, artery and nerve lie in the costal groove, from superior to inferior?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.explanation: The intercostal bundle is ordered Vein, Artery, Nerve (VAN) top-to-bottom in the costal groove of the rib above.

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.question: A chest drain should be inserted at which point relative to the ribs?
options: In the middle of the rib
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.explanation: Insert just above the upper border of the lower rib to avoid the main neurovascular bundle running in the groove of the rib above.

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.question: The 'triangle of safety' for chest-drain insertion is bordered by latissimus dorsi, pectoralis major and:
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.explanation: The triangle of safety is bounded by lat dorsi, pec major and a horizontal line at about the 5th intercostal space (nipple level).

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.question: In a tension pneumothorax, the trachea deviates in which direction, and what is the immediate management?
options: Toward the affected side; wait for CXR
Away from the affected side; immediate needle/finger decompression
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.explanation: Tension pneumothorax pushes the mediastinum and trachea AWAY from the affected side; it is a clinical diagnosis treated by immediate decompression before imaging.

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.question: The posterior intercostal arteries arise directly from which vessel?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.explanation: The posterior intercostal arteries arise from the thoracic aorta; the anterior intercostals come from the internal thoracic artery.

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.question: Which pleural layer is sensitive to pain, and via which nerves?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.explanation: The parietal pleura is pain-sensitive via the intercostal (costal) and phrenic (central diaphragmatic/mediastinal) nerves; the visceral pleura has autonomic supply and is insensitive.

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.question: Irritation of the central diaphragm characteristically refers pain to which region?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.explanation: The central diaphragm is supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3–5), so its irritation refers pain to the C4 dermatome — the shoulder tip.

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.question: Which structures pass through the T10 opening of the diaphragm?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.explanation: The T10 oesophageal hiatus transmits the oesophagus and the anterior & posterior vagal trunks (T8 = IVC, T12 = aorta + thoracic duct).

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.question: The IVC passes through the diaphragm at which vertebral level?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.explanation: The caval opening is at T8 in the central tendon (with the right phrenic nerve).

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.question: The phrenic nerve arises from which spinal roots?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.explanation: The phrenic nerve arises from C3, C4 and C5 — 'C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive.'

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.question: An inhaled peanut is most likely to lodge in which structure?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.explanation: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical, so inhaled foreign bodies preferentially enter it.

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.question: The mitral valve is best auscultated at which location?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.explanation: The mitral area is the cardiac apex — 5th intercostal space in the midclavicular line.

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.question: An inferior MI (leads II, III, aVF) usually reflects occlusion of which artery, and why can it cause heart block?
options: Right coronary artery; supplies the SA & AV nodes
Posterior descending only; no nodal supply
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.explanation: The RCA supplies the inferior wall and, in most people, the SA (~60%) and AV (~90%) nodes — so an inferior MI can cause bradyarrhythmia or heart block.

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.question: A hypotensive trauma patient has raised JVP and muffled heart sounds. What is the diagnosis?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.explanation: Beck's triad (hypotension, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds) indicates cardiac tamponade; relieve with pericardiocentesis.

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.question: The sternal angle (of Louis) lies at which vertebral level and marks which airway landmark?
options: T6/7; carina of the left bronchus
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.explanation: The sternal angle is at T4/5 and marks the 2nd costal cartilage, the tracheal bifurcation, and the limits of the aortic arch.

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.question: Which nerve, hooking under the aortic arch at the ligamentum arteriosum, causes hoarseness when compressed by an aneurysm or apical tumour?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.explanation: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the arch at the ligamentum arteriosum; compression (aortic aneurysm, enlarged left atrium, lung cancer or mediastinal nodes) paralyses the left vocal cord. When the cause is cardiovascular this is termed Ortner's (cardiovocal) syndrome.

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.question: Which organ is most at risk with a fracture of the left lower ribs (9–12)?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.explanation: Left lower rib fractures risk splenic injury; right lower rib fractures risk the liver.

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.question: The costodiaphragmatic (costophrenic) recess is clinically important because:
options: It is where the apex beat is felt
It is the lowest pleural space where effusions collect
It is the site of the cardiac notch
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.explanation: The costophrenic recess is the lowest part of the pleural cavity, not filled by lung in quiet breathing, so effusions collect there and blunt the costophrenic angle.

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.question: Which of the following is NOT a branch of the aortic arch?
options: (All three named branches arise from it)
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.explanation: The arch gives the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid and left subclavian; the right subclavian is a branch of the brachiocephalic trunk, not of the arch directly.

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.question: Superior vena cava obstruction most commonly results from:
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.explanation: SVC obstruction is most often caused by a lung cancer compressing/invading the SVC, producing facial/arm swelling, distended neck veins and Pemberton's sign.

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.question: The middle oesophageal constriction (~25 cm from the incisors) is caused by which structures?
options: The aortic arch and left main bronchus
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.explanation: The middle constriction (~25 cm) is where the aortic arch and left main bronchus cross the oesophagus; the upper is cricopharyngeus (~15 cm) and the lower is the diaphragm (~40 cm).

anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.question: A flail chest segment shows what characteristic movement?
anatomy__THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anat.explanation: A flail segment (≥2 ribs each broken in ≥2 places) moves paradoxically — drawn inward on inspiration — and the underlying lung contusion drives hypoxia.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.question: Which ribs are the 'true' ribs, attaching directly to the sternum by their own costal cartilage?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.explanation: True (vertebrosternal) ribs are 1–7; false ribs 8–10 attach to the cartilage above, and 11–12 float.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.question: The sternal angle marks the level of which costal cartilage?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.explanation: The sternal angle (manubriosternal joint) is at the 2nd costal cartilage — the landmark for counting ribs (and the T4/5 disc).

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.question: The head of a typical rib articulates with:
options: The demifacets of two adjacent vertebral bodies
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.explanation: The rib head has two facets that articulate with the demifacets of its own vertebra and the vertebra above (costovertebral joint of the head).

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.question: The tubercle of a typical rib articulates with which structure?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.explanation: The rib tubercle articulates with the transverse process of the corresponding vertebra (the costotransverse joint).

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.question: The intercostal neurovascular bundle lies in which plane?
options: Between the external and internal intercostals
Between the internal and innermost intercostals
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.explanation: The neurovascular bundle runs in the plane between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles, within the costal groove.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.question: The intercostal nerves are the anterior rami of which spinal levels (with T12 named separately)?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.explanation: Intercostal nerves are the anterior rami of T1–T11; the T12 anterior ramus is the subcostal nerve.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.question: The external intercostal muscles do what during breathing?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.explanation: External intercostals (fibres running infero-anteriorly, 'hands in pockets') elevate the ribs and assist inspiration.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.question: The internal thoracic artery arises from which vessel?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.explanation: The internal thoracic (mammary) artery is a branch of the subclavian artery.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.question: The internal thoracic artery terminates by dividing into which two arteries?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.explanation: At about the 6th intercostal space the internal thoracic artery ends as the superior epigastric and musculophrenic arteries.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.question: On the 1st rib, the scalene tubercle separates the grooves for which two structures?
options: Subclavian vein and internal jugular vein
Subclavian vein (anterior) and subclavian artery + T1 (posterior)
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.explanation: The scalene tubercle (for scalenus anterior) separates the anterior groove for the subclavian vein from the posterior groove for the subclavian artery and lower trunk (T1) of the brachial plexus.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.question: What type of joint is the first sternocostal joint (1st costal cartilage to manubrium)?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.explanation: The 1st sternocostal joint is a primary cartilaginous (synchondrosis) joint — immobile; the 2nd–7th are synovial.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.question: The pump-handle movement of the ribs increases which thoracic dimension?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.explanation: Pump-handle movement (upper ribs and sternum moving up and forward) increases the antero-posterior diameter; bucket-handle increases the transverse.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.question: A cervical rib arising from C7 can compress the lower brachial plexus and subclavian artery, producing:
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.explanation: A cervical rib narrows the thoracic outlet, compressing the lower trunk (C8/T1) and subclavian vessels — thoracic outlet syndrome.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.question: Which muscle is the principal muscle of quiet inspiration?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.explanation: The diaphragm is the main muscle of quiet inspiration; its descent increases the vertical diameter of the thorax.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.question: Which muscles are used in forced expiration?
options: Abdominal wall muscles and internal intercostals
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.explanation: Forced expiration recruits the abdominal muscles and internal intercostals; quiet expiration is passive (elastic recoil).

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.question: The posterior intercostal arteries (of the lower spaces) arise from:
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.explanation: The posterior intercostal arteries arise from the thoracic aorta (the upper two spaces from the costocervical trunk); the anterior intercostals come from the internal thoracic.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.question: The manubriosternal joint is classified as which type of joint?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.explanation: The manubriosternal joint is a secondary cartilaginous joint (symphysis), which may ossify with age (the xiphisternal joint also ossifies with age).

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.question: The floating ribs are which pair(s), and how do they end anteriorly?
options: Ribs 11–12; end freely with no anterior attachment
Rib 1 only; ends at the clavicle
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.explanation: Ribs 11 and 12 are floating (free) ribs with no anterior attachment; they also lack a neck and tubercle.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.question: The left internal thoracic artery (LIMA) is clinically prized as a:
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.explanation: The LIMA is the gold-standard conduit for coronary artery bypass grafting, typically anastomosed to the LAD.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.question: Which of the following bounds the thoracic inlet (superior thoracic aperture)?
options: The body of T1, the first ribs, and the manubrium
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.explanation: The thoracic inlet is bounded by the T1 vertebral body, the first pair of ribs and the superior border of the manubrium.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.question: Ribs 8–10 are classified as 'false' ribs because they:
options: Attach to the costal cartilage of the rib above rather than the sternum directly
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.explanation: False (vertebrochondral) ribs 8–10 attach anteriorly to the costal cartilage of the rib above, forming the costal margin, rather than to the sternum directly.

anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.question: The costal groove that carries the neurovascular bundle lies on which border of the rib?
anatomy__THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteolo.explanation: The costal groove runs along the inferior border of the rib, sheltering the intercostal vein, artery and nerve.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.question: At what level does the trachea bifurcate at the carina?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.explanation: The trachea runs from C6 and bifurcates at the carina at the T4/5 level (the sternal angle).

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.question: How many lobes does the right lung have?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.explanation: The right lung has three lobes (upper, middle, lower) separated by oblique and horizontal fissures; the left has two.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.question: At the hilum, the pulmonary artery lies anterior to the bronchus on the right and superior on the left. What is this mnemonic?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.explanation: 'RALS' — the pulmonary artery is Right Anterior, Left Superior relative to the main bronchus.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.question: What makes a bronchopulmonary segment individually resectable?
options: It has its own pleural covering
It shares a bronchus with the lobe
It has its own segmental bronchus and artery
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.explanation: Each bronchopulmonary segment has its own tertiary (segmental) bronchus and segmental artery, so it can be surgically removed as a unit.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.question: Which vessels supply oxygenated blood to the lung tissue itself (not for gas exchange)?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.explanation: The bronchial arteries (from the thoracic aorta) nourish the lung parenchyma; the pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood for gas exchange.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.question: The fossa ovalis in the right atrium is a remnant of which fetal structure?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.explanation: The fossa ovalis marks the closed foramen ovale, the fetal shunt between the atria.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.question: The moderator band of the right ventricle carries which conduction structure?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.explanation: The moderator band (septomarginal trabecula) carries the right bundle branch to the anterior papillary muscle.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.question: Which cardiac chamber has the thickest myocardial wall?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.explanation: The left ventricle has the thickest wall as it pumps blood into the high-pressure systemic circulation.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.question: The atrioventricular valves are prevented from prolapsing by which structures?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.explanation: Chordae tendineae tether the AV valve cusps to the papillary muscles, preventing prolapse into the atria during systole.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.question: The coronary arteries arise from which structures?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.explanation: The right and left coronary arteries arise from the corresponding aortic sinuses just above the aortic valve.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.question: Which structure is normally the only electrical connection between the atria and the ventricles?
options: The AV node and bundle of His
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.explanation: The AV node and bundle of His are the sole conduction pathway between atria and ventricles; the fibrous skeleton insulates the rest.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.question: The SA node (the cardiac pacemaker) is located in which chamber?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.explanation: The SA node lies in the wall of the right atrium at the upper end of the crista terminalis, near the SVC opening.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.question: The right coronary artery typically supplies which nodes?
options: Both the SA (~60%) and AV (~90%) nodes
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.explanation: The RCA gives the SA nodal branch in ~60% and supplies the AV node in ~90%, so an inferior (RCA) MI can cause bradyarrhythmia/heart block.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.question: Coronary 'dominance' is determined by which artery gives off the:
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.explanation: Dominance is defined by the origin of the posterior descending artery — ~70% of people are right-dominant (PDA from the RCA).

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.question: Most of the venous blood of the heart drains into which structure?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.explanation: The coronary sinus, in the posterior atrioventricular groove, collects most cardiac venous blood and drains into the right atrium.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.question: The sensory (pain) supply of the pericardium is carried by which nerve?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.explanation: The phrenic nerve supplies the fibrous and parietal serous pericardium, so pericardial pain is referred to the shoulder/neck.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.question: Which chamber, when enlarged, can indent the oesophagus (seen on a barium swallow)?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.explanation: The left atrium lies immediately anterior to the oesophagus, so left atrial enlargement can indent it.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.question: The lower third of the oesophagus drains venous blood into which system, explaining the varices seen in chronic liver disease?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.explanation: The lower oesophageal veins drain to the left gastric vein and thus the portal system; in portal hypertension this porto-systemic anastomosis forms varices.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.question: The thymus is the site of maturation of which cells, and with which disease is it associated?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.explanation: The thymus is where T lymphocytes mature; thymic hyperplasia or thymoma is associated with myasthenia gravis.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.question: Which fissure is present in the right lung but NOT the left?
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.explanation: The horizontal fissure (separating the upper and middle lobes) is found only in the right lung; both lungs have an oblique fissure.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.question: The transverse pericardial sinus is a surgically useful space lying between the:
options: The arterial outflow and the venous inflow
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.explanation: The transverse sinus lies between the arterial outflow tracts anteriorly and the venous structures posteriorly — a surgeon can pass a clamp/ligature around the aorta and pulmonary trunk through it.

anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.question: The left anterior descending (LAD) artery principally supplies which region of the heart?
options: The anterior wall and anterior interventricular septum
anatomy__THORAX__Viscera / Organs.explanation: The LAD supplies the anterior wall of the left ventricle and the anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum; occlusion causes an anteroseptal MI (V1–V4).

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.question: The intercostal nerves are the anterior rami of which levels (with T12 named separately)?
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: The intercostal nerves are the anterior rami of T1–T11; the T12 anterior ramus is the subcostal nerve.

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.question: Which intercostal nerves also supply the anterior abdominal wall?
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: The lower intercostal nerves T7–T11 (thoraco-abdominal) plus the subcostal T12 continue onto the abdominal wall.

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.question: The T4 dermatome corresponds to which surface landmark?
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: T4 = the nipple line (T2 axilla, T6 xiphisternum, T10 umbilicus, T12/L1 groin).

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.question: The umbilicus lies at which dermatomal level?
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: The umbilicus is the T10 dermatome.

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.question: The phrenic nerve arises from which spinal roots?
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: The phrenic nerve arises from C3, C4 and C5 — the sole motor supply to the diaphragm.

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.question: What is the relationship of the phrenic nerve to the root of the lung?
options: It does not relate to the root
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: The phrenic nerve passes ANTERIOR to the lung root ('phrenic = front'); the vagus passes posterior.

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.question: The vagus nerve passes in what relationship to the lung root, and what plexus does it then form?
options: Through the root; pulmonary plexus only
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: The vagus passes posterior to the lung root and forms the oesophageal plexus (which reconstitutes as the vagal trunks).

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.question: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under which structure?
options: The aortic arch (at the ligamentum arteriosum)
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the aortic arch at the ligamentum arteriosum; the right loops under the right subclavian artery.

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.question: The vagal trunks pass through the diaphragm at which opening?
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: The anterior and posterior vagal trunks accompany the oesophagus through the oesophageal hiatus at T10.

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.question: The greater splanchnic nerve (T5–T9) synapses in which ganglion?
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: The greater splanchnic nerve (T5–T9) synapses in the coeliac ganglion; the lesser (T10–11) → aorticorenal/SMG, the least (T12) → renal plexus.

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.question: What is characteristic of the splanchnic nerves as they cross the sympathetic chain?
options: They are preganglionic fibres that pass through without synapsing
They synapse in the chain ganglia
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: The splanchnic nerves are preganglionic sympathetic fibres that pass through the chain WITHOUT synapsing, synapsing instead in the pre-aortic abdominal ganglia.

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.question: Preganglionic sympathetic neurons arise from the lateral horn of which spinal segments?
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons arise from the lateral horn of T1–L2 (the thoracolumbar outflow).

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.question: Sympathetic stimulation of the lungs (via the pulmonary plexus) produces:
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: Sympathetic activity causes bronchodilation (and vasoconstriction); the vagus causes bronchoconstriction and secretomotor effects.

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.question: Vagal (parasympathetic) stimulation of the heart produces:
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: The vagus slows the heart rate (via the cardiac plexus); sympathetic stimulation increases rate and force and dilates the coronaries.

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.question: Myocardial ischaemic pain is referred to the chest, left arm and jaw because its afferents travel with the sympathetics to which segments?
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: Cardiac visceral afferents run with the sympathetic nerves to spinal segments T1–T4/5, so pain is referred to those dermatomes (chest, medial arm, jaw).

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.question: A patient with an apical lung tumour develops ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis. What is this syndrome, and what is disrupted?
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: Horner's syndrome results from interruption of the sympathetic supply to the head (T1/stellate ganglion), classically by a Pancoast tumour.

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.question: The phrenic nerve provides sensory supply to all of the following EXCEPT:
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: The costal parietal pleura is supplied by the intercostal nerves; the phrenic supplies the central diaphragmatic + mediastinal pleura and the pericardium.

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.question: The right phrenic nerve pierces the diaphragm at which point?
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: The right phrenic nerve passes through the caval opening (T8) with the IVC; the left pierces the muscle of the left dome.

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.question: Which nerve gives a large branch that joins the brachial plexus?
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: The T1 anterior ramus gives a large branch to the brachial plexus, leaving only a small first intercostal nerve.

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.question: White rami communicantes (carrying preganglionic sympathetic fibres) are found only at which levels?
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: White rami communicantes exist only at T1–L2 (the sympathetic outflow); grey rami connect to every spinal nerve.

anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.question: The cardiac plexus receives parasympathetic fibres from which nerve?
anatomy__THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics.explanation: The vagus supplies the parasympathetic (cardio-inhibitory) fibres to the cardiac plexus; the sympathetic fibres come from the cervical and upper thoracic ganglia.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.question: Which vessels arise directly from the ascending aorta?
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.explanation: The coronary arteries arise from the aortic sinuses of the ascending aorta; the arch gives the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid and left subclavian.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.question: The three branches of the aortic arch, in order from the right, are:
options: Left subclavian, left common carotid, brachiocephalic trunk
Brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, left subclavian
Right subclavian, right common carotid, left carotid
Brachiocephalic trunk, right common carotid, right subclavian
Left common carotid, brachiocephalic trunk, left subclavian
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.explanation: From right to left: the brachiocephalic trunk, the left common carotid and the left subclavian artery.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.question: The brachiocephalic trunk divides into the:
options: Left common carotid and left subclavian
Right common carotid and right subclavian
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.explanation: The brachiocephalic (innominate) trunk divides into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.question: The aortic isthmus lies between which two structures?
options: The brachiocephalic trunk and the left carotid
The ascending aorta and the arch
The left carotid and the left subclavian
The left subclavian artery and the ligamentum arteriosum
The ligamentum arteriosum and the diaphragm
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.explanation: The aortic isthmus is the narrowed segment between the left subclavian artery and the ligamentum arteriosum — the site of coarctation and traumatic rupture.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.question: A young man is thrown from a motorbike. A widened mediastinum on CXR raises concern for traumatic aortic injury. Where is the classic rupture site?
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.explanation: Deceleration injury classically tears the aorta at the isthmus, where the mobile arch is tethered by the ligamentum arteriosum.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.question: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under which structure, related to the aorta?
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.explanation: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the aortic arch at the ligamentum arteriosum; an arch/aortic lesion here causes hoarseness.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.question: Which of the following is a PARIETAL branch of the descending thoracic aorta?
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.explanation: The posterior intercostal (and subcostal + superior phrenic) arteries are parietal branches; the bronchial, oesophageal and pericardial branches are visceral.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.question: The pulmonary arteries are unusual because they:
options: Have valves at their origin from the LA
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.explanation: The pulmonary arteries are the only arteries carrying deoxygenated blood (from the right ventricle to the lungs).

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.question: How many pulmonary veins drain into the left atrium, and what blood do they carry?
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.explanation: Four pulmonary veins (two per lung) return oxygenated blood to the left atrium — the only veins carrying oxygenated blood.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.question: The superior vena cava is formed by the union of the:
options: Right brachiocephalic vein and azygos vein
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.explanation: The SVC is formed behind the 1st right costal cartilage by the union of the right and left brachiocephalic veins.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.question: Each brachiocephalic vein is formed by the union of which two veins?
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.explanation: Each brachiocephalic vein forms at the venous angle from the internal jugular and subclavian veins.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.question: Just before it enters the right atrium, the SVC receives which vein?
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.explanation: The azygos vein arches over the right lung root and drains into the SVC just before it enters the right atrium.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.question: The inferior vena cava pierces the diaphragm at which level, with which nerve?
options: T8, with the right phrenic nerve
T8, with the left phrenic nerve
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.explanation: The IVC passes through the caval opening at T8 accompanied by the right phrenic nerve, then enters the right atrium immediately.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.question: The azygos vein arches over the root of the right lung at approximately which level to drain into the SVC?
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.explanation: The azygos vein arches forward over the right lung root at about T4 to join the SVC.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.question: The azygos venous system is clinically important chiefly because it provides a:
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.explanation: The azygos system is a key cavo-caval anastomosis, enlarging to provide collateral flow in SVC or IVC obstruction.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.question: The thoracic duct begins at which structure?
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.explanation: The thoracic duct begins at the cisterna chyli (~L1–L2) and ascends into the thorax through the aortic hiatus.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.question: The thoracic duct enters the thorax through which diaphragmatic opening?
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.explanation: The thoracic duct passes through the aortic hiatus at T12 (with the aorta and azygos vein).

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.question: At approximately which level does the thoracic duct cross from right to left?
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.explanation: The thoracic duct ascends on the right, then crosses the midline to the left at about T4/5, ending at the left venous angle.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.question: The thoracic duct drains lymph from all of the body EXCEPT the:
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.explanation: The thoracic duct drains everything except the right upper quadrant (right head/neck, right arm, right thorax), which drains via the right lymphatic duct.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.question: Into which structure does the thoracic duct terminate?
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.explanation: The thoracic duct empties into the left venous angle — the junction of the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.question: A patient with lung cancer develops facial swelling, distended neck veins and a positive Pemberton's sign. What is the diagnosis?
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.explanation: SVC obstruction (commonly by a lung cancer) causes facial/upper-limb swelling, distended non-pulsatile neck veins and a positive Pemberton's sign.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.question: A milky pleural effusion following thoracic surgery is most likely due to injury of the:
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.explanation: Thoracic-duct injury leaks chyle into the pleural space, producing a chylothorax (milky effusion).

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.question: A Stanford type A aortic dissection involves the ascending aorta and is usually managed by:
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.explanation: Type A dissection involves the ascending aorta and requires urgent surgery; type B (descending) is usually managed medically.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.question: Rib notching and radio-femoral delay in a hypertensive young patient suggest:
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.explanation: Coarctation at the aortic isthmus causes upper-limb hypertension, radio-femoral delay and rib notching from collateral intercostal vessels.

anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.question: The correct sequence of lymphatic drainage from the lung is:
anatomy__THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics.explanation: Lung lymph passes from bronchopulmonary (hilar) → tracheobronchial (carinal) → paratracheal nodes → the bronchomediastinal trunks.
